content_voiceover: This chart shows how ALL subtype distribution shifts across the age spectrum, and the key takeaway is that Ph-like ALL becomes progressively more common as patients get older within the AYA range. In standard-risk childhood ALL it makes up only about ten percent of cases, dominated instead by ETV6-RUNX1 and hyperdiploid disease. That proportion climbs through childhood high-risk and adolescent groups, peaks at nearly twenty-eight percent in young adults aged twenty-one to thirty-nine, and stays above twenty percent through the older adult groups. Ph-like ALL is biologically important because it shares a gene expression profile strikingly similar to Philadelphia-chromosome-positive ALL, activating the same JAK-STAT and kinase signaling pathways, but without the actual BCR-ABL1 rearrangement. That means these patients often respond to tyrosine kinase inhibitors or other targeted therapy directed at their specific fusion partner, even though a standard BCR-ABL1 test would come back negative. Recognizing Ph-like ALL clinically is essential because missing it means missing a targetable lesion.
keypoints: Ph-like ALL rises with age: ~10% childhood SR to ~28% young adults
Ph-like shares JAK-STAT signaling with Ph-positive ALL
No BCR-ABL1 rearrangement despite similar gene expression
Often targetable with TKI or JAK inhibitor therapy
keypoint_voiceover: Ph-like ALL is the great mimic, it behaves like Philadelphia-positive disease genomically but tests negative for BCR-ABL1, and it becomes more prevalent as patients move from childhood into the young adult range, peaking near twenty-eight percent. Always screen for it in AYA patients since it often has a targetable kinase fusion.
